The tables on this page list the arguments accepted by figspec's functions and
explain what each argument controls. Use them to compare related functions or
find the setting for a particular task. For complete instructions, return
values and runnable examples, open the function's page in the Reference
section.

## Building, checking and exporting a figure

### `fig_save()`

Save a figure at an exact size and resolution

These examples use all 234 rows of ggplot2's mpg data. Run the setup once, then open an argument below to see how it changes the export. The setup also defines a project specification to show the alternative to using a bundled journal profile.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)

p &lt;- ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = drv, shape = drv)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    x = &quot;Engine displacement (litres)&quot;,
    y = &quot;Highway fuel economy&quot;,
    colour = &quot;Drive type&quot;,
    shape = &quot;Drive type&quot;
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

report_spec &lt;- list(
  name = &quot;Research report&quot;,
  columns = list(full = 160),
  formats = &quot;png&quot;,
  dpi_min = 300,
  dpi_line_art = 600
)
</code></pre></div></details>

<table class="table fs-options-table">
<colgroup><col style="width:26%"><col style="width:74%"></colgroup>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Option</th><th scope="col">What it does</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>filename</code></td><td>Output path. The extension selects the format. With a journal and no extension, the journal's first accepted format is used.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Give the output file a name and extension. The extension selects the file format; this example writes a PNG.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_save(
  filename = file.path(tempdir(), &quot;fuel-economy.png&quot;),
  plot = p,
  width = 85,
  height = 60,
  check = FALSE
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> A real 85 × 60 mm PNG is written in R's temporary directory.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>plot</code></td><td>Figure to save. This can be a ggplot2 or patchwork object, a gtable or grid grob, a lattice plot, a Plotly or other HTML widget, a recorded base plot, or base-graphics code wrapped in a function or one-sided formula. Defaults to the last ggplot2 plot displayed.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Pass the ggplot object you want to export. Naming plot explicitly is useful in scripts that create several figures.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_save(
  file.path(tempdir(), &quot;explicit-plot.png&quot;),
  plot = p,
  width = 85,
  height = 60,
  check = FALSE
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The object stored as p is exported, regardless of which plot was displayed last.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>spec</code></td><td>Optional specification: a registry id such as &quot;cell_press&quot;, a figspec_spec, or a named list of requirements. When given, it supplies the canvas width, resolution, format and font.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Select a bundled journal or publisher profile by its registry id. This example uses PNAS. You can also supply your own project or organisational specification through this argument.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_save(
  file.path(tempdir(), &quot;pnas-figure.tiff&quot;),
  p,
  spec = &quot;pnas&quot;,
  column = &quot;small&quot;,
  check = FALSE
)

# To use your project specification instead:
# spec = report_spec,
# column = &quot;full&quot;</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The figure uses the PNAS profile and is exported as a 90 mm TIFF at 300 dpi.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>column</code></td><td>Which of the journal's stated column widths to fit. Only meaningful with spec; defaults to &quot;single&quot; when one is given.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Choose one of the widths named in the specification. The value must match a name under columns in that specification.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_save(
  file.path(tempdir(), &quot;large-pnas-figure.tiff&quot;),
  p,
  spec = &quot;pnas&quot;,
  column = &quot;large&quot;,
  check = FALSE
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The canvas is exported at the 180 mm large width recorded for PNAS.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>width</code></td><td>Canvas width. Overrides the journal's column width.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Set the width of the complete image. Use this when you already know the required canvas width.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_save(
  file.path(tempdir(), &quot;wide-figure.png&quot;),
  p,
  width = 120,
  height = 75,
  check = FALSE
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The complete image is 120 mm wide.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>height</code></td><td>Canvas height. Defaults to three quarters of the canvas width, which is a convenience, not a journal requirement.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Set the height of the complete image instead of accepting figspec's default aspect ratio.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_save(
  file.path(tempdir(), &quot;short-figure.png&quot;),
  p,
  width = 85,
  height = 50,
  check = FALSE
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The complete image is 50 mm high.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>panel_width, panel_height</code></td><td>Size of the plot area itself. A number, or &quot;max&quot; for the largest that fits the canvas. With facets or a patchwork composition this applies to each panel.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Set the physical size of the data panel. figspec measures the labels, legend and margins, then makes the canvas large enough to contain them.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_save(
  file.path(tempdir(), &quot;fixed-panel.png&quot;),
  p,
  panel_width = 62,
  panel_height = 45,
  check = FALSE
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The data panel is 62 × 45 mm; the canvas expands around it.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>units</code></td><td>Units for width, height, panel_width and panel_height.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>State the units used by every width and height in the call. Millimetres are the default; this example gives the same size in centimetres.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_save(
  file.path(tempdir(), &quot;centimetre-size.png&quot;),
  p,
  width = 8.5,
  height = 6,
  units = &quot;cm&quot;,
  check = FALSE
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The 8.5 × 6 cm request is written as an 85 × 60 mm image.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>dpi</code></td><td>Resolution. Defaults to the journal's stated minimum, or 300.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Set the raster resolution explicitly when a specification or project requires more than the 300 dpi default.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_save(
  file.path(tempdir(), &quot;high-resolution.png&quot;),
  p,
  width = 85,
  height = 60,
  dpi = 600,
  check = FALSE
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The PNG is written at 600 dpi while keeping the requested physical size.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>transform</code></td><td>Whether to apply the specification's reachable visual requirements before export. For ggplot2 and lattice this includes typography and line rules together with accessible colour and shape defaults; Plotly receives the corresponding layout and trace settings; base graphics functions and grid grobs receive specification-aware defaults. A completed recorded plot cannot be restyled and is reported as such. Set to FALSE to preserve the plot exactly as supplied.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Keep transformation on to apply the parts of the specification that the plotting system exposes. Set it to FALSE when you need to preserve the supplied appearance and use figspec only for export and checking.</p><pre><code class="language-r">preserved &lt;- fig_save(
  file.path(tempdir(), &quot;preserved-figure.png&quot;),
  p,
  spec = report_spec,
  column = &quot;full&quot;,
  transform = FALSE,
  check = FALSE
)

transformed &lt;- fig_save(
  file.path(tempdir(), &quot;transformed-figure.png&quot;),
  p,
  spec = report_spec,
  column = &quot;full&quot;,
  transform = TRUE,
  check = FALSE
)

transformed</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The transformed file applies the project specification; the preserved file retains the supplied plot styling.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>check</code></td><td>Whether to check the result and report failures as a warning. Compliance is judged only when spec is supplied.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Leave checking on to verify the saved file against the specification. The report is attached to the returned path for later inspection.</p><pre><code class="language-r">checked &lt;- fig_save(
  file.path(tempdir(), &quot;checked-pnas-figure.tiff&quot;),
  p,
  spec = &quot;pnas&quot;,
  column = &quot;small&quot;,
  art_type = &quot;colour&quot;,
  check = TRUE
)

attr(checked, &quot;figspec_report&quot;)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The file is reopened and the report identifies the PNAS axis-origin requirement as unmet, so it can be corrected before submission.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>art_type</code></td><td>Resolution category. &quot;auto&quot; classifies the live plot; explicit choices are &quot;colour&quot;, &quot;bw&quot;, &quot;line&quot;, and &quot;combination&quot;.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Tell figspec which resolution rule applies when the content type is known. Line art often requires a higher resolution than colour images.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_save(
  file.path(tempdir(), &quot;pnas-line-art.tiff&quot;),
  p,
  spec = &quot;pnas&quot;,
  column = &quot;small&quot;,
  art_type = &quot;line&quot;,
  check = FALSE
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The 1000 dpi line-art rule recorded for PNAS is used.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>...</code></td><td>Named arguments passed to the renderer selected for the figure: ggplot2::ggsave() for ggplot2-compatible figures, the graphics device for base, lattice and grid figures, webshot2::webshot() for browser raster export, or plotly::save_image() for Plotly vector export.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Pass additional graphics-device settings through to ggplot2::ggsave(). Here bg sets the exported image's background colour.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_save(
  file.path(tempdir(), &quot;blue-background.png&quot;),
  p,
  width = 85,
  height = 60,
  check = FALSE,
  bg = &quot;#EAF4F8&quot;
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The PNG is exported with a pale blue background.</p></div></details></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

### `fig_check()`

Inspect a figure and verify it against a specification

These examples check the same real plot and a TIFF exported from it. Run the setup once, then open an argument to see what figspec measures and how it reports the result.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)

p &lt;- ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = drv, shape = drv)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    x = &quot;Engine displacement (litres)&quot;,
    y = &quot;Highway fuel economy&quot;,
    colour = &quot;Drive type&quot;,
    shape = &quot;Drive type&quot;
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

pnas_file &lt;- fig_save(
  file.path(tempdir(), &quot;pnas-check-example.tiff&quot;),
  p,
  spec = &quot;pnas&quot;,
  column = &quot;small&quot;,
  art_type = &quot;colour&quot;,
  check = FALSE
)

report_spec &lt;- list(
  name = &quot;Research report&quot;,
  columns = list(full = 160),
  formats = &quot;png&quot;,
  dpi_min = 300
)
</code></pre></div></details>

<table class="table fs-options-table">
<colgroup><col style="width:26%"><col style="width:74%"></colgroup>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Option</th><th scope="col">What it does</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>x</code></td><td>A supported live figure, or a path to a figure file. Live figures include ggplot2 and patchwork objects, lattice plots, Plotly and other HTML widgets, grid grobs, recorded base plots, and base-graphics code wrapped in a function or one-sided formula.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Check either a plot that is still editable or a finished figure file. This example reopens the TIFF created in the setup and reads its saved properties.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_check(
  x = pnas_file,
  spec = &quot;pnas&quot;,
  column = &quot;small&quot;,
  art_type = &quot;colour&quot;
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The saved TIFF is reopened; its validity, width, resolution and format all pass the PNAS checks.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>spec</code></td><td>Optional specification: a registry id such as &quot;frontiers&quot;, a figspec_spec, or a named list of requirements.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Select the requirements to check against by using a bundled registry id. The argument can also accept a project or organisational specification.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_check(
  p,
  spec = &quot;pnas&quot;,
  column = &quot;small&quot;,
  dpi = 300,
  format = &quot;tiff&quot;,
  art_type = &quot;colour&quot;
)

# To check against your project requirements instead:
# spec = report_spec,
# column = &quot;full&quot;</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The editable plot is assessed against the requirements recorded for PNAS.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>column</code></td><td>Which column width the figure is intended for. One of &quot;single&quot;, &quot;onehalf&quot; or &quot;double&quot;.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>State which named publication width the figure must occupy. figspec uses the corresponding physical width from the selected profile.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_check(
  p,
  spec = &quot;pnas&quot;,
  column = &quot;medium&quot;,
  dpi = 300,
  format = &quot;tiff&quot;,
  art_type = &quot;colour&quot;
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The width check uses PNAS's recorded 110 mm medium figure width and passes.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>width, height</code></td><td>Intended output size. Defaults to the journal's width for column. Ignored when x is a file, whose real size is measured.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Give the intended canvas dimensions when checking a plot before it is exported. For a saved file, figspec reads the actual dimensions from the file instead.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_check(
  p,
  spec = &quot;pnas&quot;,
  width = 90,
  height = 60,
  units = &quot;mm&quot;,
  dpi = 300,
  format = &quot;tiff&quot;,
  art_type = &quot;colour&quot;
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The report evaluates the plot as a 90 × 60 mm figure; the width matches PNAS's small size.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>units</code></td><td>Units for width and height.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>State the units used for width and height. This example supplies the PNAS small width in centimetres.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_check(
  p,
  spec = &quot;pnas&quot;,
  width = 9,
  height = 6,
  units = &quot;cm&quot;,
  dpi = 300,
  format = &quot;tiff&quot;,
  art_type = &quot;colour&quot;
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> figspec converts 9 × 6 cm to 90 × 60 mm before applying the checks.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>dpi</code></td><td>Resolution. For a live figure, the resolution you intend to save at. For a file, the resolution it was written at, which lets figspec judge physical size for files that do not record it themselves - base R's png() and tiff() devices do not, whereas ragg does.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Give the intended resolution when checking an editable plot. For a saved raster, figspec normally reads the resolution from the file.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_check(
  p,
  spec = &quot;pnas&quot;,
  column = &quot;small&quot;,
  dpi = 300,
  format = &quot;tiff&quot;,
  art_type = &quot;colour&quot;
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The 300 dpi value meets the PNAS minimum for a colour figure.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>format</code></td><td>Output format, for example &quot;tiff&quot;. Only used when x is a live figure.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>State the format you intend to export when checking a live plot. This example deliberately proposes JPEG so the report can identify a format PNAS does not list.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_check(
  p,
  spec = &quot;pnas&quot;,
  column = &quot;small&quot;,
  dpi = 300,
  format = &quot;jpeg&quot;,
  art_type = &quot;colour&quot;
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The file-format row fails and lists the formats accepted by PNAS.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>colour_mode</code></td><td>Intended output colour model for a live figure. Defaults to &quot;RGB&quot;; fig_save() supplies &quot;CMYK&quot; when it selects a CMYK-capable vector device.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>State the colour model planned for an editable figure. This example uses RGB, which matches the Cell Press requirement.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_check(
  p,
  spec = &quot;cell_press&quot;,
  column = &quot;single&quot;,
  dpi = 300,
  format = &quot;tiff&quot;,
  colour_mode = &quot;RGB&quot;,
  art_type = &quot;colour&quot;
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The colour-mode row passes because RGB is accepted by Cell Press.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>color_mode</code></td><td>American spelling of colour_mode. Takes precedence when supplied.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Use color_mode if you prefer American spelling. It has the same effect as colour_mode.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_check(
  p,
  spec = &quot;cell_press&quot;,
  column = &quot;single&quot;,
  dpi = 300,
  format = &quot;tiff&quot;,
  color_mode = &quot;RGB&quot;,
  art_type = &quot;colour&quot;
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The American spelling produces the same passing RGB check.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>art_type</code></td><td>Which resolution rule applies. Publishers set different minimums for different kinds of artwork: Cell Press asks 300 dpi for colour or greyscale, 500 for black and white, and 1000 for line art. &quot;auto&quot; classifies a plot from what it actually draws. For a saved file, where that evidence has been lost, it applies the strictest stated rule so that an ambiguous file cannot pass under the most lenient interpretation. &quot;color&quot; is accepted as an alias for &quot;colour&quot;.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Choose the resolution rule that matches the figure's content. The same 300 dpi file passes as colour artwork but fails the stricter PNAS line-art requirement.</p><pre><code class="language-r">colour_report &lt;- fig_check(
  pnas_file, &quot;pnas&quot;,
  column = &quot;small&quot;,
  art_type = &quot;colour&quot;
)

line_report &lt;- fig_check(
  pnas_file, &quot;pnas&quot;,
  column = &quot;small&quot;,
  art_type = &quot;line&quot;
)

rbind(
  colour = colour_report[colour_report$check == &quot;Resolution&quot;, ],
  line = line_report[line_report$check == &quot;Resolution&quot;, ]
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The two rows show 300 dpi passing for colour artwork and failing against the 1000 dpi line-art rule.</p></div></details></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

### `fig_geometry()`

Measure panel and canvas dimensions

fig_geometry() measures the panel and the complete canvas. Its plot() method turns those measurements into a diagram, making it easier to see how much room is used by labels, legends and margins.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)

p &lt;- ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = drv, shape = drv)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    x = &quot;Engine displacement (litres)&quot;,
    y = &quot;Highway fuel economy&quot;,
    colour = &quot;Drive type&quot;,
    shape = &quot;Drive type&quot;
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

sized &lt;- fig_panel_size(p, width = 62, height = 45)
geometry &lt;- fig_geometry(sized)

saved &lt;- fig_save(
  file.path(tempdir(), &quot;measured-panel.png&quot;),
  p,
  panel_width = 62,
  panel_height = 45,
  check = FALSE
)
</code></pre></div></details>

<table class="table fs-options-table">
<colgroup><col style="width:26%"><col style="width:74%"></colgroup>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Option</th><th scope="col">What it does</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>x</code></td><td>For fig_geometry(), a ggplot, patchwork composition, gtable, or the value returned by fig_save(). For plot(), the figspec_geometry object returned by fig_geometry().<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Pass a plot, a panel-sized figure or the value returned by fig_save(). A panel-sized figure reports the space used on every side; a saved value preserves the exact measurements calculated during export.</p><pre><code class="language-r">geometry &lt;- fig_geometry(x = sized)
saved_geometry &lt;- fig_geometry(saved)

geometry
plot(geometry)

geometry</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The report confirms a 62 × 45 mm data panel and shows the larger canvas needed for the axes, legend and margins.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>...</code></td><td>Accepted by the plot() generic for compatibility and ignored by this method.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>You normally leave this empty. It is accepted because plot() is a generic R function; additional values do not change figspec's geometry diagram.</p><pre><code class="language-r">plot(geometry)

# Extra values are accepted for compatibility and ignored:
plot(geometry, unused = TRUE)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> Both calls return the same panel-and-canvas diagram.</p></div></details></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

### `fig_apply_spec()`

Apply a specification while building a plot

The examples start with one plot so that each argument's effect is easy to compare. fig_apply_spec() returns ggplot2 components, which are added to the plot with + while it is still editable.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)

base_plot &lt;- ggplot(
  mpg,
  aes(displ, hwy, colour = drv, shape = drv)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = &quot;Fuel economy by drive type&quot;,
    x = &quot;Engine displacement (litres)&quot;,
    y = &quot;Highway fuel economy&quot;,
    colour = &quot;Drive type&quot;,
    shape = &quot;Drive type&quot;
  )

manual_colours &lt;- c(
  &quot;4&quot; = &quot;#375A7F&quot;,
  &quot;f&quot; = &quot;#2A9D8F&quot;,
  &quot;r&quot; = &quot;#C44E52&quot;
)
manual_shapes &lt;- c(&quot;4&quot; = 15, &quot;f&quot; = 17, &quot;r&quot; = 18)

style_register(
  &quot;research_report&quot;,
  theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      legend.position = &quot;bottom&quot;,
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    ),
  description = &quot;Minimal grid with the legend below the figure&quot;
)

report_spec &lt;- list(
  name = &quot;Research report&quot;,
  font_min_pt = 10,
  min_line_pt = 0.75,
  print_greyscale = TRUE
)
</code></pre></div></details>

<tbody>
<tr><td><code>spec</code></td><td>A registry id such as &quot;cell_press&quot;, a figspec_spec, or a named list of requirements. The specification does not have to describe a journal.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Select an included journal or publisher profile by its registry id. You can also pass requirements defined for a project or organisation.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fitted &lt;- base_plot +
  fig_apply_spec(spec = &quot;cell_press&quot;)

fitted

# Or use the project requirements:

<tr><td><code>colour</code></td><td>Whether to set the colour and fill scales. Turn this off to keep a palette you have chosen yourself.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Set colour to FALSE when the plot already has a palette you need to keep. The specification's typography and shape scale still apply.</p><pre><code class="language-r">own_colours &lt;- base_plot +
  scale_colour_manual(values = manual_colours) +
  fig_apply_spec(&quot;cell_press&quot;, colour = FALSE)

own_colours</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The three chosen colours are preserved while the other figspec components are applied.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>shapes</code></td><td>Whether to set the shape scale.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Set shapes to FALSE when the plot already uses meaningful point symbols.   fig_apply_spec(&quot;cell_press&quot;, shapes = FALSE)

own_shapes</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> Shapes 15, 17 and 18 are preserved rather than replaced by the figspec shape scale.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>style</code></td><td>A house style registered with style_register(), applied underneath the journal's requirements.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Add a registered house style for the visual choices shared by a team or project. Publication requirements are applied after the style, so the style cannot weaken them.</p><pre><code class="language-r">styled &lt;- base_plot +
  fig_apply_spec(
    &quot;frontiers&quot;,
    style = &quot;research_report&quot;
  )

styled</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The plot uses the project's minimal grid and lower legend while retaining Frontiers' required typography.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>base_size</code></td><td>Base type size in points, passed to theme_spec().<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Choose the base text size when the publication allows a range. figspec still protects the recorded minimum and maximum sizes.</p><pre><code class="language-r">larger_text &lt;- base_plot +

larger_text</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> General text and axis titles use 10 pt type, while the title is capped at PNAS's 12 pt maximum.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>color</code></td><td>American spelling of colour. Takes precedence when given. R's partial matching cannot cover this one, because color is not a prefix of colour - the spellings diverge at the fifth letter.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Use color if you prefer American spelling. It has the same effect as colour and takes precedence if both spellings are supplied.</p><pre><code class="language-r">american_spelling &lt;- base_plot +
  fig_apply_spec(&quot;cell_press&quot;, color = TRUE)

american_spelling</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The same colour-safe Cell Press plot is produced using the American argument name.</p></div></details></td></tr>
