### `fig_preview()`

Preview a figure at its intended output size

A preview opens at the physical size the finished figure will occupy. This lets you judge text, symbols and detail at their intended size while the plot is still editable.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)

p &lt;- ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = drv, shape = drv)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    &quot;4&quot; = &quot;#375A7F&quot;,
    &quot;f&quot; = &quot;#2A9D8F&quot;,
    &quot;r&quot; = &quot;#C44E52&quot;
  )) +
  labs(
    title = &quot;Fuel economy by drive type&quot;,
    x = &quot;Engine displacement (litres)&quot;,
    y = &quot;Highway fuel economy&quot;,
    colour = &quot;Drive type&quot;,
    shape = &quot;Drive type&quot;
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

report_spec &lt;- list(
  name = &quot;Research report&quot;,
  columns = list(full = 160)
)
</code></pre></div></details>

<table class="table fs-options-table">
<colgroup><col style="width:26%"><col style="width:74%"></colgroup>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Option</th><th scope="col">What it does</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>plot</code></td><td>Figure to preview. Accepts the same live figure inputs as fig_save() and defaults to the last ggplot2 plot displayed.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Pass the plot you are currently refining. Naming it explicitly avoids previewing a different plot that happened to be displayed most recently.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_preview(
  plot = p,
  spec = &quot;pnas&quot;,
  column = &quot;small&quot;
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The plot opens in a 90 × 67.5 mm preview window, the recorded PNAS small size with the default height.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>spec</code></td><td>A registry id, a figspec_spec, or a named list containing the available output widths.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Select the profile that supplies the available widths. A project or organisational specification with named widths can be used in the same way.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_preview(
  p,
  spec = &quot;pnas&quot;,
  column = &quot;small&quot;
)

# Or preview at a project width:
# fig_preview(
#   p, report_spec, &quot;full&quot;
# )</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> PNAS supplies the 90 mm small-figure width; the project alternative would use its 160 mm full width.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>column</code></td><td>Which column width to preview at.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Choose one of the named widths in the selected specification. This example previews the large PNAS figure size.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_preview(
  p,
  spec = &quot;pnas&quot;,
  column = &quot;large&quot;
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The preview opens 180 mm wide instead of the 90 mm small-figure width.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>height</code></td><td>Height. Defaults to three quarters of the width.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Set the preview height when the default three-to-four proportion does not match the figure you plan to export.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_preview(
  p,
  spec = &quot;pnas&quot;,
  column = &quot;small&quot;,
  height = 60
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The preview uses the 90 mm PNAS width and the requested 60 mm height.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>units</code></td><td>Units for height.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>State the units used for height. The width still comes from the named specification entry.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_preview(
  p,
  spec = &quot;pnas&quot;,
  column = &quot;small&quot;,
  height = 6,
  units = &quot;cm&quot;
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> Six centimetres is converted to 60 mm, producing the same 90 × 60 mm preview.</p></div></details></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

## Size and align figures

### `fig_panel_size()`

Set exact dimensions for every data panel

Set the physical size of the data panel instead of setting the outer image size and accepting whatever room remains. For a faceted plot or a multi-plot composition, the requested dimensions apply to every panel.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)

p &lt;- ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = drv, shape = drv)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    &quot;4&quot; = &quot;#375A7F&quot;,
    &quot;f&quot; = &quot;#2A9D8F&quot;,
    &quot;r&quot; = &quot;#C44E52&quot;
  )) +
  labs(
    title = &quot;Fuel economy by drive type&quot;,
    x = &quot;Engine displacement (litres)&quot;,
    y = &quot;Highway fuel economy&quot;,
    colour = &quot;Drive type&quot;,
    shape = &quot;Drive type&quot;
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

faceted &lt;- p +
  facet_wrap(~drv, nrow = 1) +
  guides(colour = &quot;none&quot;, shape = &quot;none&quot;)
</code></pre></div></details>

<table class="table fs-options-table">
<colgroup><col style="width:26%"><col style="width:74%"></colgroup>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Option</th><th scope="col">What it does</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>plot</code></td><td>The plot or composition whose data panels you want to size. This can be a ggplot, a patchwork composition, or a gtable.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Pass a single plot, a faceted plot or a patchwork composition. In this three-facet example, figspec gives each data panel the requested dimensions and allows the complete canvas to grow around them.</p><pre><code class="language-r">three_panels &lt;- fig_panel_size(
  plot = faceted,
  width = 28,
  height = 40
)

fig_geometry(three_panels)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> Each of the three data panels is 28 × 40 mm; labels, facet spacing and margins are added outside those panels.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>width, height</code></td><td>The size of each data panel. Leave either value as NULL to change only the other dimension.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Set both values when the data area must have exact dimensions. You can also supply only width or only height when the other dimension should remain flexible.</p><pre><code class="language-r">sized &lt;- fig_panel_size(
  p,
  width = 62,
  height = 45
)

fig_geometry(sized)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The data panel measures exactly 62 × 45 mm, and figspec reports the larger canvas required by the title, axes, legend and margins.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>units</code></td><td>The units used for width and height.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>State whether the panel dimensions are in millimetres, centimetres or inches. Millimetres are used by default.</p><pre><code class="language-r">sized_cm &lt;- fig_panel_size(
  p,
  width = 6.2,
  height = 4.5,
  units = &quot;cm&quot;
)

fig_geometry(sized_cm)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The centimetre values are converted to the same 62 × 45 mm panel dimensions.</p></div></details></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

### `fig_panel_width()`

Find one panel width that fits every figure

Find the widest data panel that every figure in a set can use without exceeding the available canvas width. Figures with longer labels or larger legends receive more surrounding space while their data panels remain the same width.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)

base_plot &lt;- ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = drv, shape = drv)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    &quot;4&quot; = &quot;#375A7F&quot;,
    &quot;f&quot; = &quot;#2A9D8F&quot;,
    &quot;r&quot; = &quot;#C44E52&quot;
  )) +
  labs(
    x = &quot;Engine displacement (litres)&quot;,
    y = &quot;Highway fuel economy&quot;,
    colour = &quot;Drive type&quot;,
    shape = &quot;Drive type&quot;
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

figs &lt;- list(
  numeric_labels = base_plot,
  labels_with_units = base_plot +
    scale_y_continuous(
      labels = function(x) paste(x, &quot;miles per gallon&quot;)
    )
)

report_spec &lt;- list(
  name = &quot;Research report&quot;,
  columns = list(full = 150),
  formats = &quot;png&quot;
)
</code></pre></div></details>

<table class="table fs-options-table">
<colgroup><col style="width:26%"><col style="width:74%"></colgroup>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Option</th><th scope="col">What it does</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>plots</code></td><td>The plot or list of plots that should share a panel width.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Supply the figures that need matching data areas. These two plots use the same observations and scales, but the second uses much longer y-axis tick labels and therefore has less room inside the same canvas.</p><pre><code class="language-r">shared_width &lt;- fig_panel_width(
  plots = figs,
  width = 150,
  format = &quot;png&quot;
)

shared_width
attr(shared_width, &quot;per_figure&quot;)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The plot with longer tick labels sets the shared width because it is the one with less room left for its data panel.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>spec</code></td><td>A registry id, a figspec_spec, or a named list containing the available canvas widths.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Select the specification that supplies the available canvas width. It can come from figspec's registry or from a project or organisation.</p><pre><code class="language-r">cell_press_width &lt;- fig_panel_width(
  figs,
  spec = &quot;cell_press&quot;,
  column = &quot;single&quot;,
  format = &quot;tiff&quot;
)

# A project specification works in the same way:
# report_width &lt;- fig_panel_width(
#   figs, report_spec, column = &quot;full&quot;
# )</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The Cell Press profile provides an 85 mm single-column canvas; the project alternative would provide its 150 mm full width.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>column</code></td><td>Which named width in the selected specification the figures must fit.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Choose which named canvas width the complete figures must fit. A wider publication column leaves more room for every data panel.</p><pre><code class="language-r">double_column_width &lt;- fig_panel_width(
  figs,
  spec = &quot;cell_press&quot;,
  column = &quot;double&quot;,
  format = &quot;tiff&quot;
)

double_column_width</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The 174 mm Cell Press double-column canvas produces a wider shared panel than the 85 mm single-column canvas.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>width</code></td><td>The available canvas width when you are not using a named specification.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Give the available canvas width directly for a report, thesis, presentation or other project that does not use a registry profile.</p><pre><code class="language-r">report_width &lt;- fig_panel_width(
  figs,
  width = 150,
  format = &quot;png&quot;
)

report_width</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> figspec returns the widest common panel that allows both complete figures to fit within a 150 mm canvas.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>units</code></td><td>The units used for width and for the returned panel width.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>State the units used for the canvas width. The shared panel width and its per-figure values are returned in the same units.</p><pre><code class="language-r">report_width_cm &lt;- fig_panel_width(
  figs,
  width = 15,
  units = &quot;cm&quot;,
  format = &quot;png&quot;
)

report_width_cm</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The 15 cm canvas is treated as 150 mm, and the shared panel width is returned in centimetres.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>format</code></td><td>File format the figures will be written in, for example &quot;tiff&quot;. Text is measured in the font the device resolves, so measuring on the device you will actually save with is what makes the answer exact. Defaults to the specification's first accepted format.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Measure text using the graphics format you will export. Different devices can resolve fonts slightly differently, so using the intended format keeps the calculation tied to the finished files.</p><pre><code class="language-r">tiff_width &lt;- fig_panel_width(
  figs,
  spec = &quot;cell_press&quot;,
  column = &quot;single&quot;,
  format = &quot;tiff&quot;
)

tiff_width</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> Labels, legends and margins are measured on the TIFF device before the common panel width is calculated.</p></div></details></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

## Apply and reuse visual standards

### `theme_spec()`

Apply typography requirements and a visual style

Apply the type sizes and other theme-level requirements recorded in a specification while retaining control over the figure's overall visual style. The specification may belong to a publication, project or organisation.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)

base_plot &lt;- ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = drv, shape = drv)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    &quot;4&quot; = &quot;#375A7F&quot;,
    &quot;f&quot; = &quot;#2A9D8F&quot;,
    &quot;r&quot; = &quot;#C44E52&quot;
  )) +
  labs(
    title = &quot;Fuel economy by drive type&quot;,
    subtitle = &quot;All 234 vehicles in ggplot2::mpg&quot;,
    x = &quot;Engine displacement (litres)&quot;,
    y = &quot;Highway fuel economy&quot;,
    colour = &quot;Drive type&quot;,
    shape = &quot;Drive type&quot;,
    caption = &quot;Source: ggplot2::mpg&quot;
  )

style_register(
  &quot;research_report&quot;,
  theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      legend.position = &quot;bottom&quot;,
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      axis.text = element_text(size = 6)
    ),
  description = &quot;Project report style&quot;
)

report_spec &lt;- list(
  name = &quot;Research report&quot;,
  font_min_pt = 10,
  font_max_pt = 14
)
</code></pre></div></details>

<table class="table fs-options-table">
<colgroup><col style="width:26%"><col style="width:74%"></colgroup>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Option</th><th scope="col">What it does</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>spec</code></td><td>A registry id such as &quot;plos_one&quot;, a figspec_spec, or a named list of requirements.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Choose the specification whose typography rules should be applied. A registry profile and a specification written for a project or organisation are used in the same way.</p><pre><code class="language-r">publication_plot &lt;- base_plot +
  theme_spec(spec = &quot;plos_one&quot;)

# Project typography is also supported:
# project_plot &lt;- base_plot +
#   theme_spec(report_spec)

publication_plot</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> Every text element in the publication plot is kept within PLOS ONE's recorded 8–12 pt range.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>base</code></td><td>A ggplot2 theme to build on. Defaults to ggplot2::theme_bw().<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Choose the ggplot2 theme that provides the starting appearance. figspec preserves its visual choices, then applies the specification's typography requirements.</p><pre><code class="language-r">minimal_plot &lt;- base_plot +
  theme_spec(
    &quot;plos_one&quot;,
    base = theme_minimal()
  )

minimal_plot</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The plot retains the open background and grid treatment of theme_minimal(), while its text remains within the required 8–12 pt range.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>style</code></td><td>A house style to apply: a name registered with style_register(), a ggplot2 theme, or a function returning one. Styles are applied underneath the journal's requirements and can never override them.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Add a reusable project or organisational style. Visual choices that do not conflict are retained; in this example, the 6 pt axis text is raised to the publication's 8 pt minimum.</p><pre><code class="language-r">styled_plot &lt;- base_plot +
  theme_spec(
    &quot;plos_one&quot;,
    style = &quot;research_report&quot;
  )

styled_plot</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The legend remains below the plot and minor grid lines remain hidden, but the undersized axis text is corrected to 8 pt.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>base_size</code></td><td>Base type size in points. Defaults to the journal's stated minimum, or 9 pt when the journal states none.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Set the general text size when the specification allows a range. figspec still enforces any recorded minimum and maximum.</p><pre><code class="language-r">larger_plot &lt;- base_plot +
  theme_spec(
    &quot;pnas&quot;,
    base_size = 10
  )

larger_plot</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> General text uses 10 pt type and the title is limited to PNAS's recorded 12 pt maximum.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>base_family</code></td><td>Font family. Defaults to the graphics device's own font. The journal's named font is not forced here, because a family the current device cannot resolve makes the plot fail to render at all. fig_save() applies the journal's font at save time, where the device is known. Pass a family explicitly to override.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Choose a font family that is available on the system used to render the figure. Leaving this unset allows the graphics device to use its default font.</p><pre><code class="language-r">serif_plot &lt;- base_plot +
  theme_spec(
    report_spec,
    base_family = &quot;serif&quot;
  )

serif_plot</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The project figure uses the system's generic serif family while retaining the specification's 10 pt minimum text size.</p></div></details></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

### `style_register()`

Register a reusable visual style

Give a reusable name to the visual choices shared by a project, team or organisation. The registered style is available for the rest of the R session and can be applied alongside any publication or project specification.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)

p &lt;- ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = drv, shape = drv)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    &quot;4&quot; = &quot;#375A7F&quot;,
    &quot;f&quot; = &quot;#2A9D8F&quot;,
    &quot;r&quot; = &quot;#C44E52&quot;
  )) +
  labs(
    title = &quot;Fuel economy by drive type&quot;,
    x = &quot;Engine displacement (litres)&quot;,
    y = &quot;Highway fuel economy&quot;,
    colour = &quot;Drive type&quot;,
    shape = &quot;Drive type&quot;
  )

report_spec &lt;- list(
  name = &quot;Research report&quot;,
  font_min_pt = 9,
  font_max_pt = 14
)
</code></pre></div></details>

<table class="table fs-options-table">
<colgroup><col style="width:26%"><col style="width:74%"></colgroup>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Option</th><th scope="col">What it does</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>name</code></td><td>A short identifier used to apply the style later.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Choose a short, memorable identifier. Use this name later in the style argument of theme_spec() or fig_apply_spec().</p><pre><code class="language-r">style_register(
  name = &quot;research_report&quot;,
  theme = theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = &quot;bottom&quot;),
  description = &quot;Figures for research reports&quot;
)

style_list()</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> research_report appears in the session's style list and can now be applied by name.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>theme</code></td><td>The ggplot2 theme to reuse, or a function that returns one.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Supply the ggplot2 theme choices that should be reused. A function that returns a theme is also accepted when the style needs to be created at the time it is applied.</p><pre><code class="language-r">style_register(
  &quot;presentation&quot;,
  theme_classic() +
    theme(
      legend.position = &quot;bottom&quot;,
      panel.grid.major.y = element_line(
        colour = &quot;#D7E3E8&quot;,
        linewidth = 0.3
      ),
      axis.text = element_text(size = 6),
      plot.title = element_text(face = &quot;bold&quot;)
    )
)

presentation_plot &lt;- p +
  theme_spec(
    report_spec,
    style = &quot;presentation&quot;
  )

presentation_plot</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The plot uses the registered classic layout, lower legend, blue-grey grid lines and bold title; its 6 pt axis text is raised to the project's 9 pt minimum.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>description</code></td><td>An optional one-line explanation of where or why the style is used.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Add a brief explanation so collaborators can tell where the style is intended to be used when they view the registered styles.</p><pre><code class="language-r">style_register(
  &quot;manuscript&quot;,
  theme_bw(),
  description = &quot;Black-and-white manuscript figures&quot;
)

style_list()</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The style list shows manuscript together with its plain-language description.</p></div></details></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

### `style_list()`

List the visual styles available in this session

View the reusable visual styles currently available in the R session. The returned table helps you find the name to pass to theme_spec() or fig_apply_spec() and records what each style is intended for.

_This function has no arguments._

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)

style_register(
  &quot;research_report&quot;,
  theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = &quot;bottom&quot;),
  description = &quot;Figures for research reports&quot;
)

style_register(
  &quot;presentation&quot;,
  theme_classic() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = &quot;bold&quot;)),
  description = &quot;Figures for presentations&quot;
)
</code></pre></div></details>

<details class="fs-argument-example fs-function-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Call style_list() without any arguments. It returns one row for each style registered in the current session.</p><pre><code class="language-r">available_styles &lt;- style_list()
available_styles</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The table lists research_report and presentation together with their descriptions.</p></div></details>

### `style_remove()`

Remove a visual style from the current session

Remove a visual style that is no longer needed in the current R session. Other registered styles remain available, and any RDS file previously used to save the styles is left unchanged.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)

style_register(
  &quot;research_report&quot;,
  theme_minimal(),
  description = &quot;Figures for research reports&quot;
)

style_register(
  &quot;presentation&quot;,
  theme_classic(),
  description = &quot;Figures for presentations&quot;
)
</code></pre></div></details>

<table class="table fs-options-table">
<colgroup><col style="width:26%"><col style="width:74%"></colgroup>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Option</th><th scope="col">What it does</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>name</code></td><td>The registered style name, as shown by style_list().<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Use the exact style name shown by style_list(). figspec reports an error if the name is invalid or is not registered, preventing a silent no-op from being mistaken for a successful removal.</p><pre><code class="language-r">before &lt;- style_list()
removed &lt;- style_remove(
  name = &quot;presentation&quot;
)
after &lt;- style_list()

list(
  removed = removed,
  before = before,
  after = after
)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> style_remove() returns TRUE, presentation disappears, and research_report remains registered.</p></div></details></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

### `style_save()`

Save visual styles for reuse

Save the visual styles registered in the current R session when you want to reuse them later. The resulting RDS file can be loaded from a project setup script or another session you control.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)

style_register(
  &quot;research_report&quot;,
  theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = &quot;bottom&quot;),
  description = &quot;Figures for research reports&quot;
)

style_file &lt;- tempfile(fileext = &quot;.rds&quot;)
</code></pre></div></details>

<table class="table fs-options-table">
<colgroup><col style="width:26%"><col style="width:74%"></colgroup>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Option</th><th scope="col">What it does</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>path</code></td><td>The RDS file to create.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Choose a project-controlled .rds file. figspec writes and validates a temporary copy before replacing an existing file, and it refuses directories and symbolic links.</p><pre><code class="language-r">saved_path &lt;- style_save(
  path = style_file
)

file.info(saved_path)[, c(&quot;size&quot;, &quot;isdir&quot;)]</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The RDS file is created and contains the styles currently registered in the session.</p></div></details></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

### `style_load()`

Load saved visual styles

Restore visual styles saved in an earlier session. Loaded styles are added to those already registered, allowing a project or organisation to keep a consistent figure style without recreating it by hand.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)

style_register(
  &quot;research_report&quot;,
  theme_minimal(),
  description = &quot;Figures for research reports&quot;
)
style_file &lt;- tempfile(fileext = &quot;.rds&quot;)
style_save(style_file)
style_remove(&quot;research_report&quot;)

style_register(
  &quot;dynamic_style&quot;,
  function() theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = getOption(
      &quot;figspec.legend.position&quot;,
      &quot;bottom&quot;
    )),
  description = &quot;Style that reads a project option&quot;
)
function_file &lt;- tempfile(fileext = &quot;.rds&quot;)
style_save(function_file)
style_remove(&quot;dynamic_style&quot;)
</code></pre></div></details>

<table class="table fs-options-table">
<colgroup><col style="width:26%"><col style="width:74%"></colgroup>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Option</th><th scope="col">What it does</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>path</code></td><td>The RDS file previously created by style_save().<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Load an RDS file created by style_save(). The file must be non-empty, no larger than 10 MB and contain valid named styles. Use only files you created or received through a source you trust.</p><pre><code class="language-r">loaded_names &lt;- style_load(
  path = style_file
)

style_list()</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> research_report is restored and can again be applied by name in the current session.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>allow_functions</code></td><td>Whether to permit stored theme functions. Defaults to FALSE.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Leave this FALSE for ordinary saved themes. Set it to TRUE only when a trusted file contains a theme function, because that function is executable R code.</p><pre><code class="language-r"># Without explicit permission, this file is refused:
# style_load(function_file)

loaded_functions &lt;- style_load(
  function_file,
  allow_functions = TRUE
)

style_list()</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> dynamic_style is loaded only after executable theme functions are explicitly permitted.</p></div></details></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

### `fig_tag_panels()`

Add and format labels for every panel

Add clear, consistent labels to faceted plots and multi-plot compositions. figspec can follow a recorded publication requirement or use a label style chosen for a report, presentation or other project.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)

base_plot &lt;- ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = drv, shape = drv)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    &quot;4&quot; = &quot;#375A7F&quot;,
    &quot;f&quot; = &quot;#2A9D8F&quot;,
    &quot;r&quot; = &quot;#C44E52&quot;
  )) +
  labs(
    x = &quot;Engine displacement (litres)&quot;,
    y = &quot;Highway fuel economy&quot;,
    colour = &quot;Drive type&quot;,
    shape = &quot;Drive type&quot;
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

faceted &lt;- base_plot +
  facet_wrap(~drv, nrow = 1) +
  guides(colour = &quot;none&quot;, shape = &quot;none&quot;)

city_plot &lt;- ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, cty, colour = drv, shape = drv)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = &quot;City driving&quot;,
    x = &quot;Engine displacement (litres)&quot;,
    y = &quot;City fuel economy&quot;
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = &quot;none&quot;)

highway_plot &lt;- base_plot +
  labs(title = &quot;Highway driving&quot;) +
  theme(legend.position = &quot;none&quot;)

composition &lt;- patchwork::wrap_plots(
  city_plot,
  highway_plot,
  ncol = 2
)

report_spec &lt;- list(
  name = &quot;Research report&quot;,
  panel_labels = &quot;numbers&quot;
)
</code></pre></div></details>

<table class="table fs-options-table">
<colgroup><col style="width:26%"><col style="width:74%"></colgroup>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Option</th><th scope="col">What it does</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>plot</code></td><td>A faceted ggplot or a patchwork composition to label.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Pass a faceted plot or a composition made from separate plots. figspec places one label on every visible part using the appropriate labelling method for that kind of figure.</p><pre><code class="language-r">labelled_composition &lt;- fig_tag_panels(
  plot = composition,
  level = &quot;A&quot;
)

labelled_composition</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The two plots in the composition are labelled (A) and (B) through patchwork's native tag system.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>spec</code></td><td>A registry id, a figspec_spec, or a named list containing the panel-label requirements.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Select the specification that supplies the required label style. This may be a registry profile or a specification created for a project or organisation.</p><pre><code class="language-r">cell_press_panels &lt;- fig_tag_panels(
  faceted,
  spec = &quot;cell_press&quot;
)

fig_check(cell_press_panels, &quot;cell_press&quot;)

# A project specification works in the same way:
# fig_tag_panels(faceted, report_spec)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The three facets receive capital labels and the Cell Press panel-label check passes.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>level</code></td><td>Label vocabulary: &quot;A&quot;, &quot;a&quot;, &quot;1&quot;, &quot;I&quot; or &quot;i&quot;. An explicit value overrides the specification; fig_check() will report a failure if the choice conflicts with a stated requirement.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Choose capital letters, lower-case letters, numbers, or upper- or lower-case Roman numerals. An explicit choice takes precedence over a specification, and fig_check() reports any resulting conflict.</p><pre><code class="language-r">numbered_panels &lt;- fig_tag_panels(
  faceted,
  level = &quot;1&quot;
)

numbered_panels</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The three facets are labelled (1), (2) and (3).</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>open, close</code></td><td>The characters placed before and after each label. Parentheses are used by default.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Change the characters surrounding each label. Use empty strings when no brackets are wanted.</p><pre><code class="language-r">labels_with_stops &lt;- fig_tag_panels(
  faceted,
  level = &quot;a&quot;,
  open = &quot;&quot;,
  close = &quot;.&quot;
)

labels_with_stops</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The labels appear as a., b. and c. instead of (a), (b) and (c).</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>strips</code></td><td>Whether to retain facet-strip headings. This is ignored for a patchwork composition.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Keep facet-strip headings when they convey information that the panel labels do not replace. Facet strips are removed by default.</p><pre><code class="language-r">panels_with_strips &lt;- fig_tag_panels(
  faceted,
  level = &quot;A&quot;,
  strips = TRUE
)

panels_with_strips</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The (A)–(C) labels are added while the original drive-type headings remain above the facets.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>x, y, hjust, vjust</code></td><td>The position and alignment of labels inside each faceted panel.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Move labels within faceted panels. Infinite x and y values anchor them to a panel edge, while hjust and vjust control the inset from that edge.</p><pre><code class="language-r">labels_at_top_right &lt;- fig_tag_panels(
  faceted,
  level = &quot;A&quot;,
  x = Inf,
  y = Inf,
  hjust = 1.2,
  vjust = 1.4
)

labels_at_top_right</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> Every label is placed just inside the upper-right corner of its data panel.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>...</code></td><td>Additional label settings passed to ggplot2::geom_text(), such as size, fontface, family, or colour.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Pass additional text settings to ggplot2::geom_text() when the panel labels need a particular size, weight, font or colour.</p><pre><code class="language-r">emphasised_labels &lt;- fig_tag_panels(
  faceted,
  level = &quot;A&quot;,
  size = 4,
  fontface = &quot;bold&quot;,
  family = &quot;sans&quot;,
  colour = &quot;#183A4A&quot;
)

emphasised_labels</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The panel labels are drawn in bold, 4 mm, dark blue-grey sans-serif text.</p></div></details></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

### `spec_linewidth()`

Use line widths that meet a specification

Convert a minimum line weight recorded in points into the value expected by ggplot2's linewidth argument. This prevents a direct point value from being interpreted on the wrong scale and producing lines that are too thick or too thin.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)

line_plot &lt;- ggplot(economics, aes(date, unemploy)) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = &quot;Number of unemployed people&quot;,
    caption = &quot;Source: ggplot2::economics&quot;
  ) +
  theme_spec(&quot;frontiers&quot;, base = theme_minimal())

report_spec &lt;- list(
  name = &quot;Annual report&quot;,
  min_line_pt = 1.25
)
</code></pre></div></details>

<table class="table fs-options-table">
<colgroup><col style="width:26%"><col style="width:74%"></colgroup>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Option</th><th scope="col">What it does</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>spec</code></td><td>A registry id, a figspec_spec, or a named list containing the required minimum line width.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Choose the specification that states the minimum line weight. A registry profile and a project or organisational specification are handled in the same way.</p><pre><code class="language-r">required_width &lt;- spec_linewidth(
  spec = &quot;frontiers&quot;
)

before &lt;- line_plot +
  geom_line(
    linewidth = 0.5,
    colour = &quot;#2A9D8F&quot;
  ) +
  labs(title = &quot;Before: ggplot2 linewidth 0.5&quot;)

after &lt;- line_plot +
  geom_line(
    linewidth = required_width,
    colour = &quot;#2A9D8F&quot;
  ) +
  labs(title = &quot;After: Frontiers 2 pt minimum&quot;)

comparison &lt;- patchwork::wrap_plots(
  before,
  after,
  ncol = 2
)

comparison

# A project specification works as well:
# spec_linewidth(report_spec)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The first line measures about 1.07 pt and fails the Frontiers minimum; the second measures exactly 2 pt and passes.</p></div></details></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

## Colour and visual distinction

### `colour_safety_check()`

Check whether a figure's colours remain distinguishable

Examine the colours used to represent data before exporting the figure. figspec checks any colour rules in the selected specification and also reports whether the colours remain distinct in greyscale and under common forms of colour-vision deficiency. When colour is not the only visual cue, it records that as well.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)

unsafe_plot &lt;- ggplot(
  mpg,
  aes(displ, hwy, colour = drv)
) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    &quot;4&quot; = &quot;#D62728&quot;,
    &quot;f&quot; = &quot;#2CA02C&quot;,
    &quot;r&quot; = &quot;#1F77B4&quot;
  )) +
  labs(
    title = &quot;Colour is the only cue&quot;,
    x = &quot;Engine displacement (litres)&quot;,
    y = &quot;Highway fuel economy&quot;,
    colour = &quot;Drive type&quot;
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

safer_plot &lt;- ggplot(
  mpg,
  aes(displ, hwy, colour = drv, shape = drv)
) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    &quot;4&quot; = &quot;#000000&quot;,
    &quot;f&quot; = &quot;#0072B2&quot;,
    &quot;r&quot; = &quot;#E69F00&quot;
  )) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(
    &quot;4&quot; = 16,
    &quot;f&quot; = 17,
    &quot;r&quot; = 15
  )) +
  labs(
    title = &quot;Colour and shape identify each group&quot;,
    x = &quot;Engine displacement (litres)&quot;,
    y = &quot;Highway fuel economy&quot;,
    colour = &quot;Drive type&quot;,
    shape = &quot;Drive type&quot;
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

report_spec &lt;- list(
  name = &quot;Research report&quot;,
  avoid_colour_pairs = list(c(&quot;red&quot;, &quot;green&quot;)),
  print_greyscale = TRUE
)
</code></pre></div></details>

<table class="table fs-options-table">
<colgroup><col style="width:26%"><col style="width:74%"></colgroup>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Option</th><th scope="col">What it does</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>plot</code></td><td>A ggplot object. Use the editable plot rather than an exported file so that figspec can inspect the colours actually mapped to data.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Supply the editable ggplot that you want to assess. The first example relies on a red-green contrast; the second replaces that pairing and also uses different shapes, so readers have another way to identify the groups.</p><pre><code class="language-r">unsafe_report &lt;- colour_safety_check(
  plot = unsafe_plot,
  spec = &quot;cell_press&quot;
)

safer_report &lt;- colour_safety_check(
  plot = safer_plot,
  spec = &quot;cell_press&quot;
)

patchwork::wrap_plots(
  unsafe_plot,
  safer_plot,
  ncol = 2
)

unsafe_report
safer_report</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The red-green plot fails the recorded Cell Press colour-pair rule; the revised plot passes it and uses shape as an additional cue.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>spec</code></td><td>The specification to check against. Supply a registry id, a figspec_spec, or a named list containing the colour and reproduction requirements for a publication, project or organisation.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Choose the publication, project or organisational specification whose rules should be applied. The same colours can fail one specification while remaining an advisory finding under another that does not state that rule.</p><pre><code class="language-r">cell_press_report &lt;- colour_safety_check(
  unsafe_plot,
  spec = &quot;cell_press&quot;
)

frontiers_report &lt;- colour_safety_check(
  unsafe_plot,
  spec = &quot;frontiers&quot;
)

project_report &lt;- colour_safety_check(
  unsafe_plot,
  spec = report_spec
)

cell_press_report
frontiers_report
project_report</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The red-green pairing is graded as a failure for Cell Press and the project specification; for Frontiers it is reported as unspecified because that profile records no such rule.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>threshold</code></td><td>The smallest perceptual difference that figspec will accept between two colours, measured as CIE Delta-E 2000. The default is 10; raising it makes the distinction test stricter. This setting controls the analysis and does not create a publication requirement that the selected specification does not state.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Set how different two colours must appear before figspec treats them as distinct. A higher value is stricter. This affects the colour analysis, but it does not turn the chosen cutoff into a rule from the source.</p><pre><code class="language-r">grey_plot &lt;- ggplot(
  mpg,
  aes(displ, hwy, colour = drv)
) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    &quot;4&quot; = &quot;#777777&quot;,
    &quot;f&quot; = &quot;#999999&quot;,
    &quot;r&quot; = &quot;#BBBBBB&quot;
  )) +
  labs(
    x = &quot;Engine displacement (litres)&quot;,
    y = &quot;Highway fuel economy&quot;,
    colour = &quot;Drive type&quot;
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

standard_cutoff &lt;- colour_safety_check(
  grey_plot,
  spec = &quot;royal_society&quot;,
  threshold = 10
)

more_strict &lt;- colour_safety_check(
  grey_plot,
  spec = &quot;royal_society&quot;,
  threshold = 15
)

standard_cutoff
more_strict</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> At 10, one pair of greys is too similar; at 15, two pairs are too similar. Both fail the Royal Society greyscale requirement, while the stricter cutoff identifies the additional close pair.</p></div></details></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

### `color_safety_check()`

Check whether a figure's colours remain distinguishable

The same function as `colour_safety_check()`, under the other spelling. Its options are identical.

| Option | What it does |
|:--------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `plot` | A ggplot object. Use the editable plot rather than an exported file so that figspec can inspect the colours actually mapped to data. |
| `spec` | The specification to check against. Supply a registry id, a figspec_spec, or a named list containing the colour and reproduction requirements for a publication, project or organisation. |
| `threshold` | The smallest perceptual difference that figspec will accept between two colours, measured as CIE Delta-E 2000. The default is 10; raising it makes the distinction test stricter. This setting controls the analysis and does not create a publication requirement that the selected specification does not state. |

### `figspec_palettes()`

List the colour palettes included with figspec

See which palettes figspec provides before choosing one for a plot. The catalogue distinguishes palettes for separate categories from palettes for ordered values, explains where each works best and records its source. These are optional design tools rather than publication requirements.

_This function has no arguments._

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)
</code></pre></div></details>

<details class="fs-argument-example fs-function-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Print the catalogue to compare the palettes, then draw their colours as swatches. Eight colours are shown for the fixed Okabe-Ito palette and for each sequential ramp so that their different structures are visible.</p><pre><code class="language-r">available_palettes &lt;- figspec_palettes()
available_palettes

swatches &lt;- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(seq_len(nrow(available_palettes)), function(i) {
    palette_id &lt;- available_palettes$id[[i]]
    data.frame(
      palette = available_palettes$name[[i]],
      position = seq_len(8),
      colour = figspec_palette(palette_id, 8)
    )
  })
)

ggplot(swatches, aes(position, 1, fill = colour)) +
  geom_tile(width = 0.96, height = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~palette, ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq_len(8)) +
  coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(x = &quot;Colour position&quot;) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(size = 11, face = &quot;bold&quot;),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 9),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8),
    panel.spacing.y = grid::unit(4, &quot;mm&quot;)
  )</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The catalogue lists one fixed eight-colour qualitative palette and two sequential palettes that can generate any requested number of colours; the swatches show the colours and lightness progression in each.</p></div></details>

### `figspec_palette()`

Get colours from a figspec palette

Retrieve the colours from one of figspec's palettes as hexadecimal values. The returned vector can be used in a ggplot2 manual scale, a base R plot or any other function that accepts R colours.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)

mpg_six_classes &lt;- subset(
  mpg,
  class != &quot;2seater&quot;
)

base_plot &lt;- ggplot(
  mpg_six_classes,
  aes(displ, hwy)
) +
  labs(
    x = &quot;Engine displacement (litres)&quot;,
    y = &quot;Highway fuel economy&quot;
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
</code></pre></div></details>

<table class="table fs-options-table">
<colgroup><col style="width:26%"><col style="width:74%"></colgroup>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Option</th><th scope="col">What it does</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>palette</code></td><td>The id of the palette to use, as listed by figspec_palettes().<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Select a palette by its id from figspec_palettes(). Okabe-Ito is used here because vehicle class is a set of separate categories rather than an ordered measurement.</p><pre><code class="language-r">class_colours &lt;- figspec_palette(
  palette = &quot;okabe_ito&quot;,
  n = length(unique(mpg_six_classes$class))
)

class_plot &lt;- base_plot +
  geom_point(
    aes(colour = class, shape = class),
    size = 2,
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = class_colours) +
  labs(
    title = &quot;Fuel economy by vehicle class&quot;,
    colour = &quot;Vehicle class&quot;,
    shape = &quot;Vehicle class&quot;
  )

class_plot</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> Six Okabe-Ito colours are returned and applied to six vehicle classes; shape provides a second way to identify them.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>n</code></td><td>The number of colours to return. When omitted, a sequential palette returns five colours and a fixed palette returns all of its colours. Cividis and Viridis can generate any requested number; a fixed palette returns an error rather than recycling a colour for two groups.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Ask for exactly as many colours as the data needs. Sequential palettes such as Cividis and Viridis generate the requested number, while a fixed palette stops with a clear error if the request exceeds its capacity instead of silently reusing colours.</p><pre><code class="language-r">displacement_band &lt;- cut(
  mpg_six_classes$displ,
  breaks = seq(1, 7, by = 1),
  include.lowest = TRUE,
  ordered_result = TRUE
)
number_of_bands &lt;- nlevels(displacement_band)
band_colours &lt;- figspec_palette(
  &quot;cividis&quot;,
  n = number_of_bands
)

band_plot &lt;- base_plot +
  geom_point(
    aes(colour = displacement_band),
    size = 2,
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = band_colours) +
  labs(
    title = &quot;An ordered Cividis ramp&quot;,
    colour = &quot;Displacement band&quot;
  )

band_plot

# A fixed palette is never recycled:
# figspec_palette(&quot;okabe_ito&quot;, n = 9)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> Six distinct colours are generated for the six ordered displacement bands. Asking Okabe-Ito for nine colours would stop because that fixed palette contains eight.</p></div></details></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

### `scale_colour_figspec()`

Apply a figspec palette to point and line colours

Add a figspec palette directly to the colour scale of a ggplot. This affects the colour of points, lines and outlines; it does not control the interiors of bars or other filled shapes.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)

mpg_six_classes &lt;- subset(
  mpg,
  class != &quot;2seater&quot;
)

colour_base &lt;- ggplot(
  mpg_six_classes,
  aes(displ, hwy)
) +
  labs(
    x = &quot;Engine displacement (litres)&quot;,
    y = &quot;Highway fuel economy&quot;
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
</code></pre></div></details>

<table class="table fs-options-table">
<colgroup><col style="width:26%"><col style="width:74%"></colgroup>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Option</th><th scope="col">What it does</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>palette</code></td><td>The id of the figspec palette to use. See figspec_palettes() for the available choices and their recommended uses.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Choose a palette by its id. The example maps six vehicle classes to the qualitative Okabe-Ito palette and also uses shape so that colour is not the only way to identify a class.</p><pre><code class="language-r">class_plot &lt;- colour_base +
  geom_point(
    aes(colour = class, shape = class),
    size = 2,
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  scale_colour_figspec(
    palette = &quot;okabe_ito&quot;
  ) +
  labs(
    title = &quot;Fuel economy by vehicle class&quot;,
    colour = &quot;Vehicle class&quot;,
    shape = &quot;Vehicle class&quot;
  )

class_plot</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The scale requests six colours from Okabe-Ito and applies one to each vehicle class; the colour and shape legends describe the same groups.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>...</code></td><td>Additional settings for the discrete scale, such as its legend title, labels, limits, missing-value colour or guide. These are passed to ggplot2::discrete_scale().<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Pass ordinary ggplot2 scale settings to change the legend title and labels, control their order or set the appearance of missing values. The palette still supplies the colours.</p><pre><code class="language-r">labelled_plot &lt;- colour_base +
  geom_point(
    aes(colour = drv),
    size = 2,
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  scale_colour_figspec(
    palette = &quot;okabe_ito&quot;,
    name = &quot;Drive layout&quot;,
    breaks = c(&quot;f&quot;, &quot;r&quot;, &quot;4&quot;),
    labels = c(
      &quot;Front-wheel drive&quot;,
      &quot;Rear-wheel drive&quot;,
      &quot;Four-wheel drive&quot;
    ),
    na.value = &quot;#777777&quot;
  ) +
  labs(title = &quot;A publication-ready legend&quot;)

labelled_plot</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The plot keeps the Okabe-Ito colours while showing a clearly titled legend with the three drive types written out and placed in the requested order.</p></div></details></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

### `scale_color_figspec()`

Apply a figspec palette to point and line colours

The same function as `scale_colour_figspec()`, under the other spelling. Its options are identical.

| Option | What it does |
|:--------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `palette` | The id of the figspec palette to use. See figspec_palettes() for the available choices and their recommended uses. |
| `...` | Additional settings for the discrete scale, such as its legend title, labels, limits, missing-value colour or guide. These are passed to ggplot2::discrete_scale(). |

### `scale_fill_figspec()`

Apply a figspec palette to filled areas

Add a figspec palette to the fill scale of a ggplot. Use it for the interiors of bars, boxes, areas and filled point shapes; use scale_colour_figspec() for points, lines and outlines.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>

library(ggplot2)

fill_base &lt;- ggplot(
  mpg,
  aes(class, fill = drv)
) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    x = &quot;Vehicle class&quot;,
    y = &quot;Number of models&quot;
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1))
</code></pre></div></details>

See figspec_palettes() for the available choices and their recommended uses.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Choose the palette used inside the bars or other filled shapes. This example uses three Okabe-Ito colours for the three vehicle drive types.</p><pre><code class="language-r">filled_bars &lt;- fill_base +

These are passed to ggplot2::discrete_scale().<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Pass ordinary ggplot2 scale settings to control the fill legend. Here the drive types are ordered deliberately and their abbreviated data values are replaced with labels readers can understand.</p><pre><code class="language-r">labelled_bars &lt;- fill_base +

### `scale_shape_figspec()`

Apply distinct shapes to categorical points

Add a tested set of distinct point shapes to a ggplot. Shape can reinforce colour so that groups remain identifiable when colours are difficult to distinguish or the figure is reproduced in greyscale.

library(ggplot2)

shape_base &lt;- ggplot(

  aes(displ, hwy, shape = drv, fill = drv)
) +

    size = 2.6,
    colour = &quot;#243642&quot;,
    stroke = 0.8,
    alpha = 0.85
  ) +
  scale_fill_figspec(&quot;okabe_ito&quot;) +
  labs(
    x = &quot;Engine displacement (litres)&quot;,
    y = &quot;Highway fuel economy&quot;,
    shape = &quot;Drive type&quot;,
    fill = &quot;Drive type&quot;
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
</code></pre></div></details>

<table class="table fs-options-table">

<tbody>
<tr><td><code>...</code></td><td>Additional settings for the discrete scale, such as its legend title, labels, limits, missing-value shape or guide. These are passed to ggplot2::discrete_scale().<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Pass ordinary ggplot2 scale settings to replace coded values with reader-friendly legend labels, control their order or change the symbol used for missing values.</p><pre><code class="language-r">labelled_shapes &lt;- ggplot(

<tr><td><code>style</code></td><td>The kind of marks to use: &quot;solid&quot; for solid symbols, &quot;hollow&quot; for outlines, or &quot;filled&quot; for symbols whose interior and outline colours can be controlled separately. ### `figspec_shapes()`

Get a set of distinct point shapes

Retrieve distinct ggplot2 shape codes for a manual scale or another plotting function. figspec supplies a short, deliberate set and stops instead of recycling symbols when more shapes are requested than readers can reliably distinguish.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)

shape_plot &lt;- function(shape_values, title) {
  ggplot(
    mpg,
    aes(displ, hwy, shape = drv, fill = drv)
  ) +
    geom_point(
      size = 2.6,
      colour = &quot;#243642&quot;,
      stroke = 0.8,
      alpha = 0.85
    ) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = shape_values) +
    scale_fill_figspec(&quot;okabe_ito&quot;) +
    labs(
      title = title,
      x = &quot;Engine displacement (litres)&quot;,
      y = &quot;Highway fuel economy&quot;,
      shape = &quot;Drive type&quot;,
      fill = &quot;Drive type&quot;
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
}
</code></pre></div></details>

<table class="table fs-options-table">
<colgroup><col style="width:26%"><col style="width:74%"></colgroup>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Option</th><th scope="col">What it does</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>n</code></td><td>The number of shapes needed, usually the number of groups in the data. Up to six solid, six hollow or five separately filled shapes are available.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Request one shape for each group in the data. Deriving the number from the data keeps the manual scale complete if the set of groups changes.</p><pre><code class="language-r">number_of_drive_types &lt;- length(unique(mpg$drv))
drive_shapes &lt;- figspec_shapes(
  n = number_of_drive_types
)

drive_plot &lt;- shape_plot(
  drive_shapes,
  &quot;One distinct shape per drive type&quot;
)

drive_shapes
drive_plot</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> Three groups produce the shape codes 16, 17 and 15, which are applied to all 234 observations without recycling a symbol.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>style</code></td><td>The kind of marks to return: &quot;solid&quot; for solid symbols, &quot;hollow&quot; for outlines, or &quot;filled&quot; for shapes 21 to 25, whose interior and outline colours can be controlled separately.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Choose solid marks, hollow outlines or symbols with separately controlled fills and outlines. The comparison uses the same data, dimensions and colours so that only the shape family changes.</p><pre><code class="language-r">solid_shapes &lt;- figspec_shapes(3, style = &quot;solid&quot;)
hollow_shapes &lt;- figspec_shapes(3, style = &quot;hollow&quot;)
filled_shapes &lt;- figspec_shapes(3, style = &quot;filled&quot;)

solid_plot &lt;- shape_plot(solid_shapes, &quot;Solid&quot;)
hollow_plot &lt;- shape_plot(hollow_shapes, &quot;Hollow&quot;)
filled_plot &lt;- shape_plot(filled_shapes, &quot;Filled with outline&quot;)

style_comparison &lt;- patchwork::wrap_plots(
  solid_plot,
  hollow_plot,
  filled_plot,
  ncol = 3,
  guides = &quot;collect&quot;
) &amp;
  theme(legend.position = &quot;bottom&quot;)

style_comparison

# Requests beyond a set's capacity stop with guidance:
# figspec_shapes(7, style = &quot;solid&quot;)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The comparison uses codes 16, 17 and 15 for solid marks; 1, 2 and 0 for hollow marks; and 21, 24 and 22 for marks with separately controlled fills and outlines.</p></div></details></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

### `figspec_linetypes()`

Get a set of distinct line types

Retrieve distinct line patterns for a manual scale. Adding line type to colour gives readers a second way to follow each series when the figure is reproduced in greyscale or two colours appear similar.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)

economic_series &lt;- economics_long
number_of_series &lt;- length(unique(economic_series$variable))

line_base &lt;- ggplot(
  economic_series,
  aes(date, value01, group = variable)
) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = &quot;Value, rescaled within each series&quot;,
    caption = &quot;Source: ggplot2::economics_long&quot;
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = &quot;bottom&quot;)
</code></pre></div></details>

<table class="table fs-options-table">
<colgroup><col style="width:26%"><col style="width:74%"></colgroup>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Option</th><th scope="col">What it does</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>n</code></td><td>The number of line types needed, usually the number of series in the data. Up to six are available.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Request one line type for each series in the data. The before plot uses colour alone; the after plot applies the returned patterns to the same 2,870 observations without changing the data, scales or colours.</p><pre><code class="language-r">line_patterns &lt;- figspec_linetypes(
  n = number_of_series
)

before &lt;- line_base +
  geom_line(
    aes(colour = variable),
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  scale_colour_figspec(&quot;okabe_ito&quot;) +
  labs(
    title = &quot;Before: colour is the only cue&quot;,
    colour = &quot;Economic series&quot;
  )

after &lt;- line_base +
  geom_line(
    aes(colour = variable, linetype = variable),
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  scale_colour_figspec(&quot;okabe_ito&quot;) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = line_patterns) +
  labs(
    title = &quot;After: colour and line type&quot;,
    colour = &quot;Economic series&quot;,
    linetype = &quot;Economic series&quot;
  )

before_report &lt;- colour_safety_check(
  before,
  &quot;royal_society&quot;
)
after_report &lt;- colour_safety_check(
  after,
  &quot;royal_society&quot;
)

line_comparison &lt;- patchwork::wrap_plots(
  before,
  after,
  ncol = 2,
  guides = &quot;collect&quot;
) &amp;
  theme(legend.position = &quot;bottom&quot;)

line_patterns
line_comparison
before_report[before_report$check == &quot;Redundant coding&quot;, ]
after_report[after_report$check == &quot;Redundant coding&quot;, ]

# More than six patterns stops with guidance:
# figspec_linetypes(7)</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The five series receive solid, dashed, dotted, dot-dash and long-dash lines. The colour-safety report changes from colour being the only cue to confirming that line types still distinguish the series.</p></div></details></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

### `spec_style_palette()`

Retrieve a recorded house-style palette

Retrieve an optional palette recorded as part of a specification's house style. This may describe a publication, project or organisation. A recorded palette is a visual preference rather than a requirement, and figspec does not invent one when the specification contains none.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)

report_spec &lt;- list(
  name = &quot;Annual research report&quot;,
  house_style = list(
    palette = c(
      &quot;Four-wheel drive&quot; = &quot;#1D3557&quot;,
      &quot;Front-wheel drive&quot; = &quot;#2A9D8F&quot;,
      &quot;Rear-wheel drive&quot; = &quot;#E76F51&quot;
    )
  )
)
</code></pre></div></details>

<table class="table fs-options-table">
<colgroup><col style="width:26%"><col style="width:74%"></colgroup>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Option</th><th scope="col">What it does</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>spec</code></td><td>The specification whose house-style palette should be retrieved. Supply a registry id, a figspec_spec, or a named list. It may describe a publication, project or organisation.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Supply a registry profile or your own specification. The project specification below returns its three recorded colours; PLOS ONE demonstrates the explicit no-palette response from a bundled profile.</p><pre><code class="language-r">no_recorded_palette &lt;- spec_style_palette(
  &quot;plos_one&quot;
)

report_palette &lt;- spec_style_palette(
  spec = report_spec
)

names(report_palette) &lt;- c(&quot;4&quot;, &quot;f&quot;, &quot;r&quot;)

house_style_plot &lt;- ggplot(
  mpg,
  aes(displ, hwy, colour = drv, shape = drv)
) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = report_palette,
    breaks = c(&quot;f&quot;, &quot;r&quot;, &quot;4&quot;),
    labels = c(
      &quot;Front-wheel drive&quot;,
      &quot;Rear-wheel drive&quot;,
      &quot;Four-wheel drive&quot;
    )
  ) +
  scale_shape_figspec(
    breaks = c(&quot;f&quot;, &quot;r&quot;, &quot;4&quot;),
    labels = c(
      &quot;Front-wheel drive&quot;,
      &quot;Rear-wheel drive&quot;,
      &quot;Four-wheel drive&quot;
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = &quot;A project's recorded house style&quot;,
    x = &quot;Engine displacement (litres)&quot;,
    y = &quot;Highway fuel economy&quot;,
    colour = &quot;Drive layout&quot;,
    shape = &quot;Drive layout&quot;
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

report_palette
house_style_plot</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The project specification returns its three named colours and applies them to the 234 observations. PLOS ONE returns NULL with a message because no house-style palette is recorded for that profile.</p></div></details></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

## Find and use specifications

### `spec_list()`

Browse available specification profiles

Browse the specification profiles available to figspec. Most bundled profiles apply across a publisher's journal portfolio, while others record requirements for an individual journal or publication type, so the table reaches substantially more publications than its row count suggests.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
all_profiles &lt;- spec_list()
</code></pre></div></details>

<table class="table fs-options-table">
<colgroup><col style="width:26%"><col style="width:74%"></colgroup>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Option</th><th scope="col">What it does</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>discipline</code></td><td>An optional character vector of discipline tags, such as &quot;physics&quot; or c(&quot;health&quot;, &quot;medicine&quot;). Matching is case-insensitive, and a profile is included when it has at least one requested tag.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Leave the filter as NULL to see every profile, or supply one or more discipline tags. Matching is case-insensitive, and a profile is kept when it has at least one of the requested tags.</p><pre><code class="language-r">all_profiles &lt;- spec_list(
  discipline = NULL
)

physics_profiles &lt;- spec_list(
  discipline = &quot;physics&quot;
)

health_profiles &lt;- spec_list(
  discipline = c(&quot;health&quot;, &quot;medicine&quot;)
)

all_profiles[, c(
  &quot;id&quot;, &quot;name&quot;, &quot;publisher&quot;, &quot;disciplines&quot;,
  &quot;single_mm&quot;, &quot;double_mm&quot;, &quot;dpi_min&quot;,
  &quot;verified_on&quot;, &quot;origin&quot;
)]
physics_profiles[, c(&quot;id&quot;, &quot;name&quot;, &quot;disciplines&quot;)]
health_profiles[, c(&quot;id&quot;, &quot;name&quot;, &quot;disciplines&quot;)]</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The bundled registry contains 29 profiles. Filtering returns the two physics profiles and five profiles tagged for health or medicine without changing the registry itself.</p></div></details></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

### `spec_get()`

Retrieve or create a specification

Retrieve a specification from figspec's registry or create one from a named list maintained by your project or organisation. The resulting object works with the same building, exporting and verification functions regardless of where its requirements came from.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)

project_requirements &lt;- list(
  name = &quot;Clinical research report&quot;,
  columns = list(single = 80, full = 160),
  dpi_min = 300,
  formats = c(&quot;png&quot;, &quot;pdf&quot;),
  font_min_pt = 9
)
</code></pre></div></details>

<table class="table fs-options-table">
<colgroup><col style="width:26%"><col style="width:74%"></colgroup>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Option</th><th scope="col">What it does</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>spec</code></td><td>The specification to use: a registry id such as &quot;plos_one&quot;, an existing figspec_spec, or a named list containing at least a non-empty name. Use spec_list() to browse the available registry ids. The specification does not have to describe a journal.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Supply a registry id, an existing specification object or your own named list. The example retrieves Cell Press guidance, confirms that an existing object passes through unchanged, and applies a project specification to a real plot.</p><pre><code class="language-r">publisher_spec &lt;- spec_get(
  &quot;cell_press&quot;
)

same_spec &lt;- spec_get(
  publisher_spec
)

project_spec &lt;- spec_get(
  project_requirements
)

project_plot &lt;- ggplot(
  mpg,
  aes(displ, hwy, colour = drv, shape = drv)
) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = &quot;Clinical research report figure&quot;,
    x = &quot;Engine displacement (litres)&quot;,
    y = &quot;Highway fuel economy&quot;,
    colour = &quot;Drive layout&quot;,
    shape = &quot;Drive layout&quot;
  ) +
  fig_apply_spec(
    project_spec,
    base_size = 12
  )

project_report &lt;- fig_check(
  project_plot,
  spec = project_spec,
  column = &quot;full&quot;,
  height = 95,
  dpi = 300,
  format = &quot;png&quot;
)

publisher_spec
identical(same_spec, publisher_spec)
project_spec
project_plot
project_report</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> Cell Press is retrieved with its recorded source and review date; the existing object is unchanged; and the project list becomes a specification whose width, resolution, format and type-size checks pass on the real plot.</p></div></details></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

### `fig_width()`

Look up a figure width

Retrieve a figure width from a publication, project or organisational specification. Using the recorded value keeps the figure's dimensions tied to the same specification used to build, export and verify it.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
<div class="fs-argument-example-body"><pre><code class="language-r">
library(ggplot2)

cell_press_spec &lt;- spec_get(&quot;cell_press&quot;)
report_spec &lt;- spec_get(list(
  name = &quot;Clinical research report&quot;,
  columns = list(half = 80, full = 160),
  formats = &quot;png&quot;,
  dpi_min = 300
))

width_plot &lt;- ggplot(
  mpg,
  aes(displ, hwy, colour = drv, shape = drv)
) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = &quot;Fuel economy by engine size&quot;,
    x = &quot;Engine displacement (litres)&quot;,
    y = &quot;Highway fuel economy&quot;,
    colour = &quot;Drive layout&quot;,
    shape = &quot;Drive layout&quot;
  ) +
  fig_apply_spec(cell_press_spec, base_size = 10)
</code></pre></div></details>

<table class="table fs-options-table">
<colgroup><col style="width:26%"><col style="width:74%"></colgroup>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Option</th><th scope="col">What it does</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>spec</code></td><td>The specification to use: a registry id such as &quot;cell_press&quot;, a figspec_spec, or a named list of requirements.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Supply a registry id, an existing specification object or a named list of requirements. The example retrieves one width from Cell Press and another from a project specification created in R.</p><pre><code class="language-r">publisher_width &lt;- fig_width(
  &quot;cell_press&quot;,
  column = &quot;single&quot;
)

project_width &lt;- fig_width(
  report_spec,
  column = &quot;full&quot;
)

publisher_width
project_width</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The Cell Press single-column width is 85 mm. The project specification returns its recorded full width of 160 mm.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>column</code></td><td>Name of the required width, such as &quot;single&quot;, &quot;double&quot; or &quot;triple&quot;. The available names come from the specification.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Choose one of the width names recorded in the specification. Here the Cell Press single-column width is used to export a real figure, and the saved TIFF is reopened to confirm that its physical width passes the same requirement.</p><pre><code class="language-r">fig_columns(cell_press_spec)

output_file &lt;- file.path(
  tempdir(),
  &quot;cell-press-single-width.tiff&quot;
)

saved_file &lt;- fig_save(
  output_file,
  width_plot,
  spec = cell_press_spec,
  column = &quot;single&quot;,
  height = 70,
  dpi = 300,
  check = FALSE
)

saved_check &lt;- fig_check(
  saved_file,
  spec = cell_press_spec,
  column = &quot;single&quot;,
  dpi = 300
)

saved_check[
  saved_check$check == &quot;Width&quot;,
  c(&quot;requirement&quot;, &quot;actual&quot;, &quot;status&quot;)
]</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> Cell Press records widths of 85, 114 and 174 mm. The exported image targets the 85 mm single-column width, and its saved-file width check passes.</p></div></details></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>units</code></td><td>Unit for the returned width: &quot;mm&quot;, &quot;cm&quot; or &quot;in&quot;.<details class="fs-argument-example"><summary>See how to use it</summary><div class="fs-argument-example-body"><p>Request the result in millimetres, centimetres or inches. Only the unit changes; all three values below describe the same physical width.</p><pre><code class="language-r">equivalent_widths &lt;- c(
  mm = fig_width(cell_press_spec, &quot;single&quot;, &quot;mm&quot;),
  cm = fig_width(cell_press_spec, &quot;single&quot;, &quot;cm&quot;),
  inches = fig_width(cell_press_spec, &quot;single&quot;, &quot;in&quot;)
)

equivalent_widths</code></pre><p class="fs-example-result"><strong>Result:</strong> The same Cell Press width is returned as 85 mm, 8.5 cm or approximately 3.35 inches.</p></div></details></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

### `fig_columns()`

List the available figure widths

See which named figure widths a specification provides before choosing one for a plot. The names are not universal: some sources use single and double, others add choices such as onehalf, triple, half or full.

<details class="fs-function-setup"><summary>Run the example setup</summary>
